blocks.text: At 03:00 a night-shift doctor opens a patient's notes and finds a single line from the previous afternoon: "Chest pain, looks better, plan as before." There is no date, no time, no signature, and no clue what "as before" refers to. A clear note is the main way a team passes information safely between its members.

blocks.markdown: A **clinical note** is the contemporaneous record of a patient encounter in the medical record. It serves several purposes: it lets other clinicians continue care safely, it shows your reasoning, and it forms the legal record of what happened. A good note is **accurate, timely, legible, structured and honest about what is observed and what is interpreted**.

blocks.title: Contemporaneous record
blocks.text: A **contemporaneous** note is written at the time of the encounter or as soon as possible afterwards. If written later, it should say so and state the time of the encounter and the time of writing.

blocks.markdown:
### The minimum identifiers of any entry

Every entry should have:

- the **patient's identifiers** (name, date of birth and hospital or record number, usually on each page or screen),
- the **date** and **time** (24-hour clock is preferred to avoid confusion between morning and evening),
- the **author's name**, **designation** and a **signature** (and registration number or bleep number where required),
- **legible** text; on paper, handwriting that another person can read, in black ink where local policy requires.

Because entries accumulate chronologically, an undated or unsigned entry cannot be placed in the sequence or traced to its author.

blocks.caption: Features of a well written entry
rows: Places the entry in the sequence of care
Allows the author to be traced
A consistent format such as history, examination, impression, plan
Prevents opinion being read as fact

blocks.markdown:
### Structuring the content

A common structure is the **SOAP** format:

- **S**ubjective: what the patient tells you (history, symptoms in their own words where helpful).
- **O**bjective: what you observe and measure (vital signs, examination findings, results).
- **A**ssessment: your interpretation, diagnosis or differential diagnosis.
- **P**lan: investigations, treatment, who you have informed, and when to review.

A new admission note expands this into the full history framework, followed by examination, impression and plan.

blocks.title: Turning a vague entry into a structured note
blocks.prompt: A student writes: "Mr Okoye feels better today. Looks well. Chest fine." The patient is a 62-year-old man admitted with chest pain. At 09:30 the student recorded: no pain since midnight; pulse 72 regular; blood pressure 128/78 mmHg; chest clear on auscultation. Rewrite as a SOAP note.

steps.text: Add identifiers, the date, and the time (09:30) at the start of the entry.
S: "No chest pain since midnight" is the patient's report and goes under Subjective.
O: pulse 72 per minute and regular, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg and clear chest sounds are measured or observed, so they go under Objective with units.
A: "Improving" is an interpretation. Write it as such under Assessment, linked to the findings above.
P: add the plan and review time, then sign with your name and designation.

blocks.answer: 09:30, S: no chest pain since midnight. O: pulse 72/min regular, BP 128/78 mmHg, chest clear. A: symptomatically improving. P: continue monitoring, review later today. Signed with name and designation.

blocks.markdown:
### Fact versus interpretation

A **fact** is something you saw, heard, measured or were told. An **interpretation** is your judgement about what that fact means. Both belong in a note, but they must be labelled so that a later reader can see which is which.

- Fact: "Smell of alcohol on breath; speech slurred; unable to walk in a straight line."
- Interpretation: "Intoxicated."

Writing only the interpretation can mislead a later reader who does not know what it is based on. For example, "appears drunk" in a patient with head injury or hypoglycaemia could delay the correct diagnosis.

blocks.title: Separating fact from interpretation
blocks.prompt: Classify each phrase as fact or interpretation: (a) "Patient is aggressive." (b) "Patient shouted and pushed the chair away."

steps.text: Phrase (a) is a label that reflects the writer's judgement and has no observable detail, so it is an interpretation.
Phrase (b) describes what was seen and heard, so it is a fact.
Recommended practice: record the behaviour (b), and, if you wish, add your interpretation separately.

blocks.answer: (a) is interpretation; (b) is fact; record observable behaviour and label interpretation.

items: Write the note as soon as possible after the encounter.
Use the patient's words in quotation marks where they add information.
Use standard abbreviations only and avoid ambiguous ones.
Record negative findings that matter, such as "no neck stiffness".
Do not write offensive or speculative comments about the patient.

blocks.title: Never use fillers like "as before"
blocks.text: Phrases such as "plan as before" or "no change" are meaningless to a colleague who did not read the earlier entry. State the plan or finding in full.

blocks.title: OSCE tip
blocks.text: If asked to write a note in an examination, start with date, time and identifiers, use a clear structure, and finish with your name, role and signature. Mark facts and interpretations separately.

points: A clinical entry must be dated, timed, legible and signed, with the author's name and role, and identifiers for the patient.
Structure notes consistently, for example with SOAP or a full history, examination, impression and plan.
Record facts (what you saw, heard, measured) separately from interpretation, and label each clearly.
Avoid vague phrases, non-standard abbreviations and offensive or speculative comments.

questions.stem: Which set of items is the minimum required for a valid entry in the medical record?

options.text: Date, time, legible content, and the author's signature and designation
Date and the patient's diagnosis only
The author's initials and the ward name only
Time only, because the date is on the front cover

questions.correctOptionText: Date, time, legible content, and the author's signature and designation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: each entry must be traceable and placeable in time.
distractorRationale.b: A diagnosis alone does not identify the author or time of entry.
distractorRationale.c: Initials and ward do not give date, time or role.
distractorRationale.d: Every entry needs its own date.

questions.explanation: A clinical entry that lacks date, time, a legible text or a signature cannot be reliably placed in the sequence of care or traced to its author. Each entry must stand on its own.

questions.stem: A doctor reviews a patient at 14:10 but writes the note at 17:00 after an emergency. Which is the best practice?

options.text: Write the note with the time of the encounter and state that it was written later at 17:00
Write 14:10 only, so that it looks contemporaneous
Write nothing because the review was too long ago
Ask a colleague to write it from memory

questions.correctOptionText: Write the note with the time of the encounter and state that it was written later at 17:00

distractorRationale.b: This misrepresents when the note was written.
distractorRationale.c: A delay is not a reason to omit the record.
distractorRationale.d: Only the clinician who saw the patient can record the encounter accurately.

questions.explanation: Late entries are acceptable if they are clearly labelled with both the time of the event and the time of writing. Misstating the time would damage the credibility of the record.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a fact rather than an interpretation?

options.text: Patient is probably faking the pain

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a measurement with value, unit and time.
distractorRationale.b: A diagnosis is an interpretation of findings.
distractorRationale.c: A judgement about the patient's manner.

questions.explanation: A measured value with unit and time is an observation anyone can verify. Diagnoses and judgements about behaviour are interpretations and must be separated from the underlying observations.

questions.stem: In the SOAP format, where does the sentence "Patient says the headache started suddenly two hours ago" belong?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it reports what the patient says.

questions.explanation: The Subjective section records the patient's own account of symptoms. Examination findings, measurements and results go under Objective.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to record a patient's blood pressure in a note?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: value, unit, arm, position and time.
distractorRationale.d: Meaningless to a reader who did not see the earlier entry.

questions.explanation: A recorded measurement should include the value, unit, conditions and time so that it can be compared later. Vague words and references to earlier entries do not allow this.

questions.stem: True or false: writing only "patient is agitated" without describing what the patient did is an acceptable way to record a behavioural observation.
questions.explanation: "Agitated" is a judgement, so the underlying observations such as pacing, repeated requests to leave or raised voice should be recorded as facts. Without them later readers cannot judge the basis for your interpretation.

questions.stem: A student's entry reads: "Patient drunk, refused treatment, difficult." A colleague asks her to improve it. Which revision is best?

options.text: "Alcohol smell on breath, speech slurred, stated 'I'm not staying' and left the cubicle at 22:40; plan explained and risks discussed."

questions.correctOptionText: "Alcohol smell on breath, speech slurred, stated 'I'm not staying' and left the cubicle at 22:40; plan explained and risks discussed."

distractorRationale.a: Correct: observable facts, the patient's own words, time, and what was explained.

questions.explanation: The best revision gives observable facts, time and what the clinician did. It avoids labels and speculation and records the patient's words and the information given.

questions.stem: Write the elements that every clinical entry should contain, and explain why each is important.
markingGuide: Legible handwriting or clear typed text
Date and time place the entry in the sequence of care
Signature allows the author to be traced
questions.explanation: Each element has a role: sequencing, traceability or safety. A strong answer links every item to its purpose rather than listing them.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman attends clinic with two days of sore throat and fever. Describe how you would structure the clinical note of the encounter using the SOAP format, giving one example of content for each heading.
markingGuide: Subjective: the patient's account, for example two days of sore throat and fever
Objective: measured findings such as temperature, throat appearance, lymph nodes
Assessment: interpretation such as likely pharyngitis
Plan: actions such as advice, investigations, safety-netting, review
Identifiers, date, time and signature included
questions.explanation: SOAP separates what the patient tells you from what you find, what you think and what you will do. The best answers show that each heading has distinct content.

questions.stem: Explain why a clinical note should distinguish between fact and interpretation, giving an example of a statement that mixes the two and a corrected version.
markingGuide: Later readers can check the basis for a judgement
Interpretations may be wrong and can bias subsequent care
Facts can be verified and used legally
Example of a mixed statement, such as "anxious and manipulative"
Corrected version records observed behaviour and the patient's words
Interpretation stated separately and clearly labelled
questions.explanation: A note is read by people who will rely on it without having met the patient. Separating observation from opinion lets them weigh the evidence themselves and guards against bias.
